name: George Washington Carver
teaser: The American botanist born into slavery who turned peanuts, sweet potatoes, and soybeans into hundreds of products to revive exhausted Southern soils. He gave his discoveries away, asking only that farmers use them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Carver promoted crop rotation with nitrogen-fixing legumes to restore cotton-drained soil. Write about his peanut research at Tuskegee and how his work helped poor farmers.

name: Luther Burbank
teaser: The American horticulturist who bred over 800 plant varieties, from the Burbank potato to the Shasta daisy. His relentless selection showed what patient human hands could coax from nature — before genes were even named.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Burbank crossed and selected plants to create new varieties. Write about two of his creations, like the plumcot or the Shasta daisy, and how his methods foreshadowed modern breeding.

name: Nikolai Vavilov
teaser: The Russian botanist who crisscrossed the globe collecting seeds and pinpointed the regions where crops were born — the Vavilov centers. He defended genetics against state dogma, was arrested, and starved to death in prison.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Vavilov's expeditions built the world's greatest seed bank and mapped centers of crop origin. Write why he defied Lysenko's rejection of genetics and what happened to him.

name: Eugene Odum
teaser: The American ecologist who made ecosystems the unit of study and wrote the textbook that founded ecosystem ecology. His famous aphorism: 'the organism is only the visible product — the ecosystem is the real unit of nature.'

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Odum defined an ecosystem as organisms plus their environment exchanging energy and matter. Write about energy flow and nutrient cycling, and why his textbook shaped environmental science.

name: Arthur Tansley
teaser: The British botanist who coined the word 'ecosystem' in 1935, insisting that plants, animals, soil, and climate form one working whole. He pushed ecology from description toward a science of systems.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Tansley coined 'ecosystem' and what he meant by it. Write how his systems view differs from simply listing species, and give one example of an ecosystem in balance and disturbance.

name: Karl von Frisch
teaser: The Austrian ethologist who decoded the waggle dance — honeybees telling hive-mates the direction and distance to flowers. He shared the 1973 Nobel with Lorenz and Tinbergen for founding the science of animal behavior.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how von Frisch deciphered the waggle dance's angle and duration as a coded map to food. Write how bees communicate distance and direction, and how scientists confirmed the dance.

name: Konrad Lorenz
teaser: The Austrian zoologist who imprinted goslings to follow him, proving some behaviors are wired in at birth. His books on aggression and animal instincts made ethology famous — and him a household name.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Lorenz showed that goslings follow the first moving thing they see after hatching. Write what imprinting is, its critical period, and why his work founded the study of instinct.

name: John Tyndall
teaser: The Irish physicist who explained why the sky is blue and measured how greenhouse gases trap heat — the first solid evidence for the greenhouse effect. He also founded the science of light scattering and the sterilization of air.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Tyndall showed that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb infrared heat. Write why the sky is blue via Tyndall scattering and why his 1859 experiments matter to climate science today.

name: George de Hevesy
teaser: The Hungarian chemist who invented radioactive tracers — tagging atoms to follow them through the body and the periodic table. He discovered hafnium and, legend says, dissolved his Nobel gold medals in acid to hide them from the Nazis.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Hevesy used radioactive isotopes as tracers in biology and chemistry. Write how tracer experiments revealed metabolic pathways and how he discovered the element hafnium.

name: Emil von Behring
teaser: The German physician who found that blood serum from immunized animals could cure diphtheria — the first serum therapy and the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded in 1901.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Behring and Kitasato developed antitoxin therapy against diphtheria and tetanus. Write how passive immunization works and why his serum treatment saved thousands of children.

name: Selman Waksman
teaser: The Ukrainian-American microbiologist who combed the soil for antibiotics and found streptomycin — the first cure for tuberculosis. He coined the word 'antibiotic' and won the 1952 Nobel, though his lab's history grew bitter over credit.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Waksman's systematic search of soil microbes yielded streptomycin against TB. Write how actinomycetes produce antibiotics and why his discovery transformed treatment of the 'white plague.'

name: Howard Florey
teaser: The Australian pharmacologist who turned Fleming's forgotten mold into a lifesaving drug, racing against war to mass-produce penicillin. He and Ernst Chain shared the 1945 Nobel for making the antibiotic age real.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Florey's Oxford team purified and mass-produced penicillin during WWII. Write the steps from Fleming's mold to the wonder drug, and why Florey's work saved more lives than the bomb took.

name: Walter Reed
teaser: The American Army physician who proved yellow fever is spread by mosquitoes, not filth or touch — and proved it with volunteers who risked their lives. His work let the Panama Canal be built and reshaped tropical medicine.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Reed's carefully designed experiments in Cuba incriminated the Aedes mosquito. Write how his use of consenting volunteers and quarantine huts proved transmission beyond doubt.

name: Alexander Yersin
teaser: The Swiss-French physician who sailed to Hong Kong during the 1894 plague outbreak and isolated its bacterium, later named Yersinia pestis after him. He spent his later years exploring Vietnam's jungles and founded its medical school.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Yersin, working with a simple microscope in Hong Kong, identified the plague bacterium. Write how it spreads from rats via fleas and why his discovery made diagnosis and control possible.

name: Ronald Ross
teaser: The British physician who proved malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes, tracing the parasite through a bird's bloodstream to the mosquito's salivary glands. He won the 1902 Nobel — and later fought the disease across the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Ross found malaria parasites inside Anopheles mosquitoes and proved the transmission cycle. Write the full cycle from mosquito to human and back, and why his finding made malaria control possible.

name: Charles Nicolle
teaser: The French physician who realized typhus is carried by body lice while watching patients in a Tunisian hospital — the sick arriving in lice-infested clothes, the nurses oddly immune. He won the 1928 Nobel for the discovery.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Nicolle deduced that typhus spreads through body lice by observing hospital admissions. Write how delousing camps and the later DDT campaigns used his insight to stop typhus epidemics.

name: Virginia Apgar
teaser: The American anesthesiologist who devised the Apgar score — the 1-minute, 5-minute check of a newborn's heart rate, breathing, and reflexes — giving every baby a fair start. It has saved millions of lives since 1953.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the five Apgar criteria — Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration — each scored 0-2. Write what each checks and why assessing a newborn at 1 and 5 minutes is so valuable.

name: Charles Drew
teaser: The American surgeon who pioneered blood banks and discovered how to separate and preserve plasma, letting blood be stored and shipped. His 'blood for Britain' program saved countless lives in WWII — yet the Red Cross first refused his blood donation system due to segregation.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Drew found that plasma could be separated, dried, and safely transported. Write how his blood bank methods transformed surgery and wartime medicine, and the discrimination he faced.
